meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whatever you are, be a good one'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln. The line traces to Thackeray via Laurence Hutton’s 1897 memoir; the Lincoln credit is a 1946 invention with no source.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — most likely William Makepeace Thackeray
answer.sourceLine: There is no Lincoln speech, letter, or document that contains this line, and the first record tying it to him surfaces in 1946 — 81 years after his death. The earliest documented version, “Whatever you are, try to be a good one,” appears in Laurence Hutton’s 1897 memoir, where he recalls the novelist William Makepeace Thackeray saying it to him as a boy — though even that credit rests on how well Hutton remembered the encounter.

source.excerpt: Whatever you are, try to be a good one.
trail: Quote Investigator finds the earliest form in Laurence Hutton’s 1897 memoir, where the words are Thackeray’s: “Whatever you are, try to be a good one.”
By 1904 newspapers were printing the shortened “Whatever you are, be a good one,” still crediting Thackeray, per QI’s chronology.
The first tie to Lincoln appears only in 1946 — 81 years after his death, with no source — and Mental Floss lists it among quotes commonly misattributed to him.
source.excerptNote: As recalled by Laurence Hutton: Thackeray laid his hand on the boy’s head and asked what he meant to be; told the answer, the novelist replied with these words. The clipped modern form — “Whatever you are, be a good one” — and the Lincoln credit both came decades later.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented wording was published in 1897 (Hutton’s memoir in St. Nicholas) and the shortened form by 1904 — both well before 1931 — so the text is in the public domain in the United States. Thackeray died in 1863; Hutton in 1904.

author.name: William Makepeace Thackeray
author.heading: About William Makepeace Thackeray
author.bio: William Makepeace Thackeray was a leading Victorian novelist, best known for Vanity Fair (1847–48), a satirical panorama of English society. Born in Calcutta and educated at Cambridge, he was a rival of Dickens and a fixture of London literary life. The line credited to him survives only secondhand, in the boyhood memoir of the American essayist Laurence Hutton.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most common quotes falsely pinned on Abraham Lincoln — a feel-good line with no basis in anything he wrote or said.

items.why: No Lincoln speech, letter, or document contains this line. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest link to Lincoln is a 1946 anthology that gave no source — 81 years after his death. Mental Floss lists it among quotes commonly misattributed to him.

items.who: “be a good one” vs. “try to be a good one”
items.why: The familiar phrasing drops a word. The earliest documented form is “Whatever you are, try to be a good one”; the shorter, punchier version only took hold from about 1904, per QI.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-supported origin is William Makepeace Thackeray, recorded in Laurence Hutton’s 1897 memoir — though, as Quote Investigator cautions, that credit depends on the reliability of Hutton’s childhood memory.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Lincoln
lead: Short, warm, and quietly commanding, the line fits the folk image of Lincoln as a plain-spoken moral teacher — exactly the profile that makes him a magnet for orphan quotes. Once an unsourced 1946 anthology attached his name, reprint culture and, later, social media did the rest.

The irony is that the sentiment was never his. It reaches print through the memoir of a young American who says a visiting British novelist — Thackeray — laid a hand on his head and offered the advice. Even that is a memory recorded four decades after the fact.
context.pull: No Lincoln document contains the line; the Lincoln credit first appears in 1946.
